response: As I sit down to write about my own experiences as an only child, I'm reminded of the countless solitary birthdays I spent as a kid, surrounded by empty chairs and the weight of my parents' expectations. (In those moments, I often felt like I was shouldering the entire burden of family happiness, with no one to share the responsibility with.) But as I grew older, I began to realize that these quiet dinners with my parents were actually a blessing in disguise - they offered a space for deep, meaningful conversations that allowed us to connect on a level that was both intimate and independent. (One of my earliest memories is of my mom making me a special birthday dinner, just the two of us, and me feeling like I was the only person in the world who mattered.) As I entered adulthood, I began to understand the weight of carrying family expectations alone, and how it can shape one's approach to life's challenges and relationships. (For example, I've found that I'm more likely to take on solo projects and responsibilities, not just because I'm independent, but also because I've learned to rely on myself in a way that's hard to shake.) And yet, as I look back on my life, I realize that being an only child has also given me a unique perspective on solitude and family dynamics - (I've come to appreciate the value of alone time, but also the importance of nurturing those relationships that are truly meaningful to me.) Ultimately, I'm left wondering: (How do other only children navigate the complexities of family expectations and personal identity?)
